chartIntros.text: This is my reading of the chapters, not a finding from the sources.

p: Six areas of daily life compared at about 1825, 1925 and 2025. The premise that life looked much the same in 1925 does not hold as stated for the United States, and holds better for parts of Asia and Africa. The biggest change after 1925 is in health and numbers (my reading).
The pace of change rose over two centuries, but the measures do not show a break at 1925: output stepped up near 1900, population after 1926 and energy use after 1950 (my reading).
Children dying before 15 fell from about 1 in 2 to 4%, and life expectancy rose from 32 to 71 (1900–2021). Drug-resistant infection is one of the setbacks it records.
Food supply rose from 2,184 to 3,006 kilocalories per person per day, and French working hours fell by more than half. 673 million still faced hunger in 2024.
Adult literacy rose from about 1 in 10 people to about 88%, and internet use from 16% to 74%. 739 million adults lack basic literacy and 2.2 billion are offline.

Six features of exposure: planetary reach, speed, irreversibility, concentrated dependence, few hands and thin margins. 12,187 warheads, seven of nine planetary boundaries transgressed, and about half of food resting on synthetic nitrogen.
Nineteen events. In share terms the worst losses came earlier: the Black Death took 30–60% of Europe, against 3.0–3.7% of the world in the Second World War.
Nineteen systems. Large measured falls where the hazard is known and countable, and several defenses weakening: New START expired, the US left the WHO, the pandemic annex is unfinished.
Monitored wildlife populations fell by an average of 73% from 1970 to 2022, about a million species are threatened, and 84% of reef area met bleaching-level heat in 2023–2025.
Mass extinctions removed about 70–85% of species at a time, and recovery took roughly 6 to 75 million years.
17.6% of land and 8.4% of ocean protected against 30% targets. Humpback whales recovered to about 93% of their pre-whaling size, and fewer than half of aligned national targets are on track.
Child labour fell from 246 million to about 138 million. The richest 10% take 53% of income and the poorer half 8%. Population is projected to peak near 10.3 billion in the 2080s.
Measured scores rose for decades and now show reversals in several countries. Wisdom has no agreed measure, and the chapter gives no verdict.
1.2 billion people live with a mental disorder, one third of those with depression get formal care, and 1 in 6 people are affected by loneliness.
By V-Dem's 2026 count 74% of people live in autocracies and democracy for the average person is back at its 1978 level. Freedom House reports 20 years of decline.

The hypothesis, stated and tested six ways. Realised loss: not supported. Worst case: supported as a model result only. Reach: supported in kind. Reversibility and defenses: mixed. Dependence: cannot be compared.
Nine open items with their latest checked status and what to watch, from the pandemic annex and nuclear limits to a century-by-century tally nobody has yet built.

patterns.h3: The hypothesis is only partly borne out
p: The evidence does not show that this century has been the worst in realised loss. It does show exposure at the scale of the whole world that none of the 19 earlier events I selected matches.

patterns.h3: The gains are large and counted
p: Health, food, literacy and connection improved by wide margins, and Chapters 3 to 5 give the figures. The strains in Chapters 12 to 15 remain alongside them.

patterns.h3: The two sides are different kinds of evidence
p: Gains and past losses are counted. Much of the exposure is modelled or judged, so the two cannot be added into one balance.

patterns.h3: A narrower claim fits better than the wording
p: The best-supported form is that this is the first century in my record in which human choices carry measured or modelled effects at the scale of the whole world. That is my judgment, and the original claim can still be kept and tested.

limits: Every chapter lists its own limits and the strength of each source, and those limits carry into this overview.
Most figures are secondhand: I read pages through a summarizing tool, so check figures against the originals before citing them.
Chapter 7 relies mostly on Wikipedia, and several later chapters rely on news reports of institutional reports.
The results in Chapters 16 and 17 are my judgment, not findings from the sources.
Chapters 12 to 15 rarely reach back to 1925, so for those the two centuries cannot be compared.
Figures are current to dates between 13 and 28 October 2026, and several items, such as nuclear limits and the pandemic annex, are still moving.

claim.q: Humanity has made itself vulnerable to catastrophic outcomes through the last 100 years of advancement, unlike any other 100 years of advancement in known history.
claim.s: Tested in Chapter 16 against the evidence in the other chapters.

patterns.h3: In the United States, the premise does not hold as stated
p: By 1925 half of US households had electric power, and the car reached the same share the next year (1926). Radio had passed 10 percent. The 1925 hemline also differs sharply from the 1820s silhouette. Atlantic crossings had fallen from 23–40 days to about 5. I have household data only for the United States, so I cannot say the same of Europe; the dress and crossing rows cover Western fashion and the North Atlantic.

patterns.h3: For much of the world it holds better
p: Around 1920 the urban share was about 10 percent in both Africa and Asia, and it reached about 43 and 46 percent by 2016. In 2000, 2 in 10 people still lacked electricity and about half lacked clean cooking fuels. For these regions the large visible shift came after 1925.

patterns.h3: The largest change in the second century is in health and numbers, not in objects
p: Life expectancy was about 29 in the early 1800s and 31–32 in 1900, then 72.6–73.2 in 2019–2020. Child deaths before 15 fell from about a quarter in 1950 to 4% in 2020. This is the change a photograph of 1925 would not show.

patterns.h3: Both centuries saw the speed of the journey fall by a large factor, in different ways
p: From the 40-day westbound packet to the 1924 Mauretania, about 5 days, the time fell roughly eightfold. From 1924 to the fastest 2020 airliner crossing, about 25-fold. The second figure compares a ship with an aircraft, so it measures a change of method as much as of speed.

patterns.h3: What the evidence supports
p: My reading: 'visually similar by 1925' is better described as 'the shape of modern household life was in place in the United States by 1925, and reached much of the rest of the world after it'. What changed after 1925 was how many people shared it, how long they lived, and how fast and far they could travel.

patterns.h3: Population is the clearest acceleration, and it comes after 1925
p: It took 121 years to add the second billion and 34 for the third, then 12 each for the fifth to eighth. The projections lengthen again, to about 15 and 23 years. The time per billion has stayed at 12 years since 1974, so the fastest pace is a plateau of the late 20th and early 21st centuries.

patterns.h3: Output growth shows no step at 1925
p: On the DeLong reconstruction, world output grew about 2.6% a year in 1900–1925 and 2.7% in 1925–1950, against 0.74% a year over 1500–1900. The step up sits between the long pre-1900 average and the 20th century. I have no 1825 value and no value after 1950 from this series, so I cannot place the start of the step within the 19th century.

patterns.h3: Energy speeds up after 1950
p: Energy supply grew about 1.7% a year from 1900 to 1950 and about 3.0% from 1950 to 2000. From 2000 to 2024 it grew 1.8% a year, below the 1950–2000 rate. The measure is a rise in use, not a count of inventions.

patterns.h3: The spread of household machines did not keep getting faster
p: From 10% to about 50% of US homes, the telephone took 43 years and electric power 17. Radio took 6 in the 1920s and 30s, the refrigerator about 8, and the cell phone and the internet 8 and 9 around the turn of the 21st century. The fastest cases are spread across both centuries.

patterns.h3: What the evidence supports
p: My reading: the last century was faster than the one before on population, energy, output and travel time, but the measures do not change pace at the same date, and the speed of household adoption shows no trend. Output changes near 1900, population after 1926, energy after 1950, and travel time with the change from ship to aircraft. A neat split at 1925 describes none of them exactly.

limits: Almost every rate here is my own arithmetic on two endpoints. A compound annual rate hides movement inside the window, including the effect of the two world wars on the 1900–1950 figures.
The windows differ from 1825–1925 and 1925–2025 because the series do not have those years. Each row states the years it uses.
The world output series is a reconstruction in 1990 international dollars, with long gaps early on. I read only the six dates the Wikipedia table gives, and none after 1950.
The household adoption series is for the United States only, and the 50 percent year is the nearest value I read for the colour television, cell phone and internet rows.
The crossing times combine different ships, routes and measures, and the sailing averages have no stated year. They show orders of magnitude, not a tidy series.
Pace is measured here by what could be counted. Changes in ideas, institutions or ways of working have no series in this chapter.

items.h3: Children dying before they grow up
p: Around two centuries ago, about 1 in 2 children died before the end of puberty. By 1950 the share had fallen to around one-quarter, and by 2020 to 4%. In 2023 the UN estimated 4.8 million children died before their fifth birthday, and said child deaths had dropped by more than half since 2000.

How solid The 1800 figure is described only as 'around 1 in 2', with no exact value. The 1950 and 2020 figures are Our World in Data's. The 2023 count and the 'more than half since 2000' are from the UN's own estimate, as reported by WHO.

kv.v: In 2020, 13% of children in Nigeria and 7% in Pakistan died before 15, against 0.4% in Italy, Iceland, Japan and Norway.
Child mortality rose in South Africa and Zimbabwe in the 1990s and 2000s, largely because of HIV/AIDS.
About 1.9 million in 2023, down by over a third since 2000.

items.solid: How solid The 1800 figure is described only as 'around 1 in 2', with no exact value. The 1950 and 2020 figures are Our World in Data's. The 2023 count and the 'more than half since 2000' are from the UN's own estimate, as reported by WHO.

p: In Sweden and Finland around 1800, around 900 mothers died per 100,000 live births, and in some countries in the 19th century the figure was roughly 500 to 1,000. In most rich countries it is now below 10, a fall of 50- to 100-fold.

p: Donald Henderson estimates about 300 million people died of the disease in the 20th century. In 1967 an estimated 10 to 15 million people were infected each year while only 132,000 cases were reported. The last natural case of the milder form was in Merka, Somalia, on 26 October 1977, and the World Health Assembly certified elimination in May 1980.

p: Salk's vaccine was announced as effective in April 1955 and Sabin's oral vaccine was licensed in 1961. In the early 1980s an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 people were paralysed each year, and polio was endemic in 125 countries in 1988. The page gives 1,873 estimated paralytic cases in 2020 and 649 reported cases in 2021.
How solid The 1980s figure is an estimate and the 2021 figure is reported cases, so the two are not the same kind of count.

kv.v: Wild poliovirus cases were recorded only in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Malawi as of 2021.
The page states no percentage. My arithmetic gives a fall of about 99.4–99.5% from the early 1980s to 2020 in estimated cases.

items.solid: How solid The 1980s figure is an estimate and the 2021 figure is reported cases, so the two are not the same kind of count.

p: A 2024 study by Shattock and colleagues estimated that routine vaccinations prevented 154 million deaths worldwide in the last fifty years. Measles vaccination alone is credited with 94 million lives.

How solid These are modelled estimates, not counts. The page gives no period for the measles figure, though a related chart is titled 1974 to 2024, and it gives no coverage figures for earlier decades.

kv.v: Over 80% of infants worldwide now receive the full DTP course, a year not stated.
Measles needs coverage typically above 90% for herd immunity.

items.solid: How solid These are modelled estimates, not counts. The page gives no period for the measles figure, though a related chart is titled 1974 to 2024, and it gives no coverage figures for earlier decades.

items.h3: Pneumonia, tuberculosis and diarrhoea in the United States
p: In 1900 pneumonia, tuberculosis and diarrhoea and enteritis were the leading causes of death, and with diphtheria they caused one-third of all deaths. In 1900, 194 of every 100,000 US residents died of tuberculosis.
How solid From the CDC's account of 20th-century public health. It is about the United States only, and the page text gives no overall infectious disease death rate for 1900 or 1996.

kv.v: The CDC credits clean water, chlorination, sewage disposal and hygiene education, penicillin from the 1940s and later antimicrobials, and childhood vaccination programmes from the 1950s and 1960s.
Infectious disease mortality rose overall during the 1980s and early 1990s.

items.solid: How solid From the CDC's account of 20th-century public health. It is about the United States only, and the page text gives no overall infectious disease death rate for 1900 or 1996.

p: Global life expectancy at birth was 32 years in 1900 and 71 in 2021, according to Our World in Data, which says no region had a life expectancy above 40 in 1800. WHO puts it at 73.4 in 2019, 71.5 in the pandemic low of 2021 and 73.3 in 2023.
How solid The 1900 figure is a reconstruction and differs between sources (the earlier chapter shows 31 to 32 on one page). The 2023 figures are from a news report of WHO's October 2026 estimates.

kv.v: In 2021 life expectancy in Nigeria was thirty years lower than in Japan. Hong Kong had the highest female life expectancy, 88 years.
Healthy life expectancy was 62.8 in 2023, 0.4 years below its 2019 level.

items.solid: How solid The 1900 figure is a reconstruction and differs between sources (the earlier chapter shows 31 to 32 on one page). The 2023 figures are from a news report of WHO's October 2026 estimates.

p: Heart diseases cause a third of deaths worldwide and cancers almost one in five, together about every second death. Infectious diseases cause around 1 in 7. Neonatal and maternal deaths and accidents each account for about 4%, suicide for 1.3% and interpersonal violence for under 1%.
How solid From the Global Burden of Disease via Our World in Data. The page gives no percentage for non-communicable diseases as a whole and no figures for how the shares shifted.

kv.v: Death rates from both infectious and non-communicable diseases have fallen since 1990, communicable ones faster.

items.solid: How solid From the Global Burden of Disease via Our World in Data. The page gives no percentage for non-communicable diseases as a whole and no figures for how the shares shifted.

patterns.h3: A few named causes account for much of the change
p: The entries that carry the largest numbers are infections of childhood and birth: smallpox, polio, tuberculosis, diarrhoea and childbirth. The CDC and Our World in Data both attribute the decline to clean water, vaccines and antibiotics.

patterns.h3: Several gains came from organised campaigns
p: Smallpox and polio were attacked by programmes with a target, and the 1980 certification of smallpox elimination is the one finished case in the record.

patterns.h3: Most of the rise in life expectancy falls in the last 125 years
p: No region exceeded 40 in 1800, the world averaged 32 in 1900, and it was 71 in 2021. The chapter's data give no 1825 or 1925 figure, so the split at 1925 cannot be tested here.

patterns.h3: The gains depend on a continuing system
p: Vaccination needs coverage above 90% for measles, antibiotics lose force as resistance grows, and the UN links aid cuts to disrupted vaccination and clinic closures.

patterns.h3: The gaps between countries remain large
p: The sources show a 30-year gap in life expectancy between Nigeria and Japan in 2021, and in 2020 a share of children dying before 15 that was 13% in Nigeria against 0.4% in Italy, about 32 times higher by my division.

limits: This chapter covers only what could be counted as survival and length of life. It does not measure pain, disability or the quality of care.
The deaths 'prevented' by vaccination and the deaths 'attributable' to resistance are model estimates, not counts.
Early figures are reconstructions. The 1800 and 1900 values rest on thin records, and several are given as ranges or as 'around'.
I did not find world figures for 1825 or 1925, so the two-century split used in earlier chapters cannot be applied here.
The list is a selection of eight gains. It leaves out insulin, anaesthesia, surgery, nutrition and many other advances.

p: The FAO's measure of food supplied per person per day rose from 2,184 kilocalories in 1961 to 2,457 in 1980, 2,659 in 2000, 2,796 in 2010 and 3,006 in 2023. Supply grew substantially in Asia and Africa, and the regional gaps have been converging. In France the average food supply more than doubled over the last 300 years.
How solid The world figures are from the FAO series as compiled by Our World in Data. The page gives no regional values in its text and the French long-run figure is the only one before 1961.

kv.v: The figure counts food available at retail level and leaves out waste in homes, so people eat less than the supply. It measures energy only, not vitamins or minerals.

items.solid: How solid The world figures are from the FAO series as compiled by Our World in Data. The page gives no regional values in its text and the French long-run figure is the only one before 1961.

p: Ó Gráda calls 100 million deaths a conservative estimate for famines in the 19th century, about the same as the 20th-century total, so the 19th century was far deadlier in proportion. The deadliest 20th-century famine was in China from 1958 to 1962, an estimated 36 million deaths, or 45 million in Dikötter's estimate. Wartime famines in the Second World War killed about 25 million.

How solid Estimates differ widely: the Chinese toll is 36 or 45 million depending on the author. The page cites Devereux as calling the 20th century the highest total for any century, which sits oddly beside Ó Gráda's figure, and it gives no 21st-century total.

kv.v: The death rate from famine fell to very low levels in the second half of the 20th century. Northeast Nigeria in 2016–2019, with an estimated 340,000 deaths, is the only large famine in a democracy since 1870, according to the page.

items.solid: How solid Estimates differ widely: the Chinese toll is 36 or 45 million depending on the author. The page cites Devereux as calling the 20th century the highest total for any century, which sits oddly beside Ó Gráda's figure, and it gives no 21st-century total.

items.h3: People still without enough to eat
p: The UN estimates 8.2% of the world, about 673 million people, faced hunger in 2024, with a range of 638 to 720 million. The share was 8.5% in 2023 and 8.7% in 2022. In Africa it was over 20%, affecting 307 million people, while in Asia it fell from 7.9% in 2022 to 6.7%, or 323 million, in 2024.
How solid The 2024 figure is a UN estimate with a stated range. The page gives no hunger figure for 2000 or 2019, so I cannot show the long run.

kv.v: 512 million people could be chronically undernourished by 2030, almost 60% of them in Africa. The UN goal is to end hunger by 2030.

items.solid: How solid The 2024 figure is a UN estimate with a stated range. The page gives no hunger figure for 2000 or 2019, so I cannot show the long run.

items.h3: The long run of extreme poverty
p: Michail Moatsos estimates that about three-quarters of the world lived in extreme poverty in 1820. Our World in Data's count of people below $1.90 a day shows 965 million in 1820, 1,596 million in 1950, 1,904 million in 1990, 1,091 million in 2010 and 733 million in 2015.
How solid The chart's own page names the $1.90 line but no data source and does not say how 1820–1980s values are made. The 1820 and later figures should be read as estimates with different methods.

kv.v: The 1820 share uses a cost-of-basic-needs approach, while later figures use an income or consumption line. The two do not measure the same thing.
The count rose from 1820 to 1990 while the population also grew, and then fell.

items.solid: How solid The chart's own page names the $1.90 line but no data source and does not say how 1820–1980s values are made. The 1820 and later figures should be read as estimates with different methods.

p: The World Bank puts the number of people below $3 a day, in 2021 prices, at about 837 million in 2026, down from about 2.3 billion in 1990. Most of the decline came from East Asia and South Asia. Extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and in places affected by conflict and fragility.

How solid From the World Bank's own page, which gives a different line and different prices from the $1.90 chart above, so the two series should not be joined. The page text states no global percentage. The Our World in Data author argues that a $3 line is too high to show the incomes of the very poorest.

kv.v: Progress has slowed over the last decade, and at the current pace ending extreme poverty could take decades.

items.solid: How solid From the World Bank's own page, which gives a different line and different prices from the $1.90 chart above, so the two series should not be joined. The page text states no global percentage. The Our World in Data author argues that a $3 line is too high to show the incomes of the very poorest.

p: World output was 1,103 billion in 1900 and 4,082 billion in 1950 in 1990 international dollars on the DeLong reconstruction. Output per person was 11,275 in 1990 and 21,914 in 2025 in 2021 international dollars, and total output was about 180 trillion in 2025.
How solid Wikipedia's table gives no per-person figures before 1990. I found no world per-person series for 1825 or 1925.

kv.v: By my division, output per person in 2025 was about 1.94 times that of 1990. The 1990–2025 per-person series has a different base from the DeLong series, so I do not join them.

items.solid: How solid Wikipedia's table gives no per-person figures before 1990. I found no world per-person series for 1825 or 1925.

p: Annual hours worked per worker fell in France from 3,168 in 1870 to 1,487 in 2023, in Germany from 3,284 to 1,335, in the United Kingdom from 2,755 to 1,523 and in the United States from 3,096 to 1,789. Japan fell from 2,076 in 1950 to 1,654, while India's figure was 2,434 in 1970 and 2,383 in 2023.
How solid The page does not name the source of the series or say whether it counts full-time and part-time work alike, so the long-run values need checking before use.

kv.v: My division gives falls of 53% in France, 59% in Germany, 45% in the United Kingdom and 42% in the United States since 1870.
Workers in richer countries tend to work fewer hours than those in poorer countries, and the page notes large inequalities within and between countries.

items.solid: How solid The page does not name the source of the series or say whether it counts full-time and part-time work alike, so the long-run values need checking before use.

items.h3: Light, heat and clean fuel at home
p: Half of US households had electric power in 1925 and 90% by 1949. Worldwide, more than 1.5 billion people lacked electricity in 1998 and fewer than 1 in 10 lack it now. About two-thirds of the world cooked with clean fuels in 2020, up from about half in 2000, and in the United States nearly half of homes lacked complete plumbing in 1940 and 1% did in 1990.
How solid The US figures are from the OWID household-technology chart and the Census Bureau. The world figures are from Our World in Data's energy-access page, read through a summarizing tool.

kv.v: The first chapter gives the full series and sources.

items.solid: How solid The US figures are from the OWID household-technology chart and the Census Bureau. The world figures are from Our World in Data's energy-access page, read through a summarizing tool.

patterns.h3: Supply rose, and hunger remains
p: The calorie supply per person rose by about 38% between 1961 and 2023 on my division (2,184 to 3,006), yet 8.2% of the world still faced hunger in 2024. On these numbers the problem is not the world average.

patterns.h3: Deadly famine has become rare, and the earlier toll was large
p: The famine death rate fell to very low levels in the second half of the 20th century, and the one large recent case, Northeast Nigeria, is estimated at 340,000 deaths against tens of millions in earlier cases.

patterns.h3: The number in extreme poverty fell by about 64% since 1990 on the World Bank figures
p: From about 2.3 billion to 837 million, my division, mostly in East and South Asia. The count had risen from 1820 to 1990, as population grew.

patterns.h3: Working hours fell in the rich countries shown and hardly in India
p: The four rich countries shown cut annual hours by 42–59% since 1870. India's figure barely changed from 1970. Other countries are not shown, and the numbers do not show cause.

patterns.h3: This chapter's data do not fall on 1825 and 1925
p: Calories begin in 1961, poverty counts in 1820 and 1950, the World Bank figure in 1990 and working hours in 1870. A split at 1925 cannot be tested here.

limits: The measures cover food, money and hours, and say nothing about security, meaning or how people felt about their lives.
The poverty series use different lines, prices and methods, so the earlier and later figures should not be joined into one line.
I found no world per-person income series for 1825 or 1925. The only per-person series I read starts in 1990.
Several pages gave their data only in charts, which I read through downloaded data files and a summarizing tool. Check against the originals.
Housing beyond plumbing and electricity, clothing cost, and the price of food relative to wages are not covered here.

groups.header: Learning to read and going to school

p: Our World in Data says only one in ten people in the world could read and write in 1820 and one in five in 1870, and that more than four in five can now. UNESCO puts adult literacy at about 88% and youth literacy at 93%, up from 87% in 2000. At least 739 million adults still lack basic literacy, almost two-thirds of them women, with 347 million in Central and Southern Asia. Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest regional rate, 68.5%.

How solid The 1820 and 1870 figures have no named source on the page, and its own text says both 'one in ten remain illiterate' and 'more than 4 out of 5 can read', which it does not reconcile. The UNESCO figures come from a news report of UNESCO's estimates, with no single data year given.

kv.v: Historical estimates often count only people who could sign documents, which the page calls a very basic lower bound. Modern figures come from a yes or no question, 'Can you read and write?', which treats literacy as all or nothing.

items.solid: How solid The 1820 and 1870 figures have no named source on the page, and its own text says both 'one in ten remain illiterate' and 'more than 4 out of 5 can read', which it does not reconcile. The UNESCO figures come from a news report of UNESCO's estimates, with no single data year given.

items.h3: More children in school, many still not learning
p: Fewer than 1 in 5 adults had some basic education in 1820. Now less than 1 in 5 has none. Most children are enrolled in primary school, and girls are almost as likely as boys to be. Around 244 million children and youth were out of school in 2023 on Our World in Data's page, and a June 2025 report of UNESCO's estimate gave 272 million.
How solid The two out-of-school figures differ and come from different reports and years. The 272 million is a news report's account, and it gave no reference year.

kv.v: In many lower-income countries fewer than 20% of children reach minimum reading proficiency by the end of primary school. Adults in some poorer countries average 2 to 3 years of schooling, about a decade less than in Europe or North America.

items.solid: How solid The two out-of-school figures differ and come from different reports and years. The 272 million is a news report's account, and it gave no reference year.

items.h3: Radio, telephone and television in US homes
p: In US households radio went from 10% in 1925 to 50% in 1931 and 90% in 1947. The landline telephone took from 1903 to 1946 to reach half of homes. Colour television went from 10% in 1966 to 90% in 1985, and the internet from 10% in 1993 to a peak of 88% in 2016.
How solid From the Our World in Data household-technology chart, read from its data file. It covers the United States only, and I found no world series for these machines.

kv.v: The first chapter gives the full series and the figures for the cell phone.

items.solid: How solid From the Our World in Data household-technology chart, read from its data file. It covers the United States only, and I found no world series for these machines.

p: The first handheld cellular call was made on 3 April 1973 with a handset weighing about 2 kilograms. The first commercial automated cellular network opened in Japan in 1979, and the first commercially available handheld phone, the DynaTAC 8000x, followed in 1983. Subscriptions passed seven billion in 2014 and reached over 9.1 billion in 2024.
How solid From Wikipedia. Subscriptions count connections, not people, and the page says the 2024 total is enough for one per person on Earth. It gives no figures for the 1990s or for 2000.

kv.v: Smartphones were about half of mobile phone sales in 2024.

items.solid: How solid From Wikipedia. Subscriptions count connections, not people, and the page says the 2024 total is enough for one per person on Earth. It gives no figures for the 1990s or for 2000.

items.h3: Half the world, then three-quarters, online
p: The share of the world's people online was 16% in 2005, 30% in 2010, 60% in 2020 and 74% in 2025, about 6 billion people, with 2.2 billion still offline. The ITU puts use at 23% in low-income countries against 94% in high-income countries, and at 85% for urban residents against 58% for rural. Africa's share rose from 2% in 2005 to 37% in 2023 while Europe's went from 46% to 91%.
How solid The 2005 to 2023 figures come from Wikipedia and the 2025 figures from a summary of the ITU's Facts and Figures 2025. Pages disagree for 2023: 63% on Our World in Data and 67% on Wikipedia.

kv.v: 5G covers an estimated 55% of the world's people, 84% in high-income countries and 4% in low-income ones. Access remains unaffordable in around 60% of low- and middle-income countries.

items.solid: How solid The 2005 to 2023 figures come from Wikipedia and the 2025 figures from a summary of the ITU's Facts and Figures 2025. Pages disagree for 2023: 63% on Our World in Data and 67% on Wikipedia.

patterns.h3: The reach of reading took about two centuries
p: From about 1 in 10 in 1820 to about 88% of adults now. The early figures have no named source and count a very basic skill, so the starting point is soft.

patterns.h3: The reach of the internet took about twenty years
p: From 16% in 2005 to 74% in 2025. In US homes the internet took nine years to go from 10% to about half, as Chapter 2 shows.

patterns.h3: Access and learning are different things
p: Adult literacy is about 88%, yet in many lower-income countries fewer than 20% of children reach minimum reading proficiency by the end of primary school. Mobile subscriptions exceed the world's population, yet 2.2 billion people are offline.

patterns.h3: The gaps are along income and place
p: Low-income against high-income countries, rural against urban residents, Africa against Europe: in each pair the gap in 2023 or 2025 is between 27 and 71 points, on my subtraction of the figures above.

patterns.h3: This chapter measures access, not what people do with it
p: Whether wider access has made people wiser or less so is a different question, which the plan leaves to Chapter 13.

limits: The measures are literacy, schooling and connections. They say nothing about how much people know, how well they judge what they read, or what they use the connection for.
Early literacy estimates rest on signatures and small samples, and the pages that give them name no source.

Mobile subscriptions count connections, not people. I found no count of unique mobile users.

06-century-of-vulnerability.html.title: Century of vulnerability
06-century-of-vulnerability.html.sub: How the last hundred years built the means of global catastrophe
06-century-of-vulnerability.html.lede: Seven areas where modern technology and industry now carry a risk of catastrophic, widespread harm. Each section gives current figures and says how solid the evidence is.
06-century-of-vulnerability.html.asof: Figures current to 13 October 2026. Many come from secondary summaries; see the notes on source quality at the end.

chartIntros.text: Novel entities means synthetic chemicals, plastics and similar substances. Biogeochemical flows means nitrogen and phosphorus.

Tags: P is a primary source or an institution's own page, S is a secondary summary (news, trade press, a law-firm blog or Wikipedia). I read the pages through a summarizing tool, so check figures against the original before citing.

domains.title: Nuclear weapons
domains.solid: How solid The warhead counts are estimates by a research institute but widely used. The famine figures come from one climate model, one crop model and one fishery model, assume international trade stops entirely and do not model adaptation. Treat them as a scale, not a forecast.

domains.title: Climate and the Earth system
domains.solid: How solid The CO2 and temperature series are direct measurements. The boundary framework is a scientific proposal for where safe limits lie, not a settled threshold. Toby Ord rates the direct existential risk from climate this century at about 1 in 1,000, well below his figure for AI, so its main weight in this account is as a multiplier on food, health and conflict.

domains.title: The living world
domains.solid: How solid The report itself says the figure is not a headcount of animals lost and is especially sensitive to changes in already small populations. It is a strong signal about trend, and a weak guide to how much total wildlife remains.

domains.title: Food from one industrial process
domains.solid: How solid Estimates range from 40 to 50 percent depending on method, because breeding, irrigation and mechanization also raised yields.

domains.title: Pathogens and medicine
domains.solid: How solid The resistance and COVID figures are modeled estimates with wide ranges. Mirror life is speculative. The authors say the key components do not yet exist and that building such an organism could take 10 to 30 years.

domains.title: Advanced AI
domains.solid: How solid The tournament ran from June to October 2022, before ChatGPT's release, and its authors say it was not designed to show whether superforecasters are reliable on long-term questions. Nobody can currently measure the probability of an AI catastrophe, and the range of expert opinion is wide.

patterns.h3: Planetary reach
p: Harm can arrive everywhere at once. The atmosphere, the oceans, global supply chains and global travel do not stop at borders.

patterns.h3: Speed
p: Some failures unfold in hours, as a nuclear launch would. Others unfold in months, as a pandemic does once people can travel between continents in a day.

patterns.h3: Irreversibility
p: Some changes cannot be undone on human timescales: coral reefs past their tipping point, species lost for good, ice sheets that have begun to melt.

patterns.h3: Concentrated dependence
p: Large parts of humanity rely on a few processes or places. Synthetic fertilizer sits under about half the world's food, and one island makes most of the most advanced chips.

patterns.h3: Few hands
p: The decision or error that sets off the worst outcomes can rest with very few people. The 1983 and 1962 nuclear close calls each turned on one officer's judgment.

patterns.h3: Thin margins
p: The limits that once slowed an arms race have lapsed, and the evidence about new technologies trails the technologies themselves.

limits: AI can help produce laboratory instructions and troubleshoot experiments. It is uncertain how much this raises real-world biological risk.
Criminal groups and state-linked attackers already use AI in the preparation of cyberattacks. AI is not yet running attacks fully on its own.
Loss-of-control scenarios are possible if systems learn to evade oversight. Expert views on how likely this is vary widely, and current systems are not yet highly capable.
The report calls its core problem an evidence dilemma: the field moves fast, and evidence about new risks arrives slowly.
Nuclear war and food. The famine estimates come from smoke cooling the climate and cutting harvests, so a military event becomes a food event worldwide.

Many limits at once. Seven of nine planetary boundaries are transgressed together, and all seven are at their highest recorded levels. Fertilizer, for example, feeds about half the world while also pushing the nitrogen boundary.
The same period of tension. The 2026 Doomsday Clock statement ties together the end of nuclear limits, slow climate progress, and the uncontrolled spread of generative AI feeding disinformation.
AI and biology. The AI safety report finds that AI can assist with laboratory work, although it is unclear how much extra risk that adds.

07-record-of-catastrophes.html.sub: Nineteen events, from a volcano 74,000 years ago to COVID-19

chartIntros.text: Estimated deaths

Ranges are the lowest and highest estimates in the sources. The Atlantic slave trade bar adds deaths at sea to deaths inside Africa after capture, which is my arithmetic. The Americas, Toba, Tambora and the Bronze Age collapse have no death totals that I could confirm, so they are left out of this chart. Smallpox covers a whole century.
Share of a population lost

The bases differ, so read each label. A region, a city, a country and the world are not the same denominator. The Bengal and COVID-19 shares are my arithmetic, using about 60.3 million people in Bengal and about 7.8 billion people in the world.

Tags: P is a primary source or an institution's own page, S is a secondary summary (here, mostly Wikipedia). I read the pages through a summarizing tool, so check figures against the original works before citing.

p: Sumatra, Indonesia

The eruption rated VEI 8, the top of the scale, and is the largest known explosive eruption of the Quaternary. One theory holds that it caused a volcanic winter of six to ten years and cut the human population to a few thousand people.

How solid Very contested. Models bring cooling back to normal within about five years, lake records in Malawi show no major ecological change, and stone tools in India look the same above and below the ash. Some researchers consider the theory disproved.

kv.v: About 3,800 cubic kilometres of erupted material by the latest estimate. Earlier estimates ran from 2,000 to 6,000.
Natural.
Unknown. The population bottleneck was proposed by Ambrose in 1998.

items.solid: How solid Very contested. Models bring cooling back to normal within about five years, lake records in Malawi show no major ecological change, and stone tools in India look the same above and below the ash. Some researchers consider the theory disproved.

p: Eastern Mediterranean and Near East

Between the late 13th and early 12th centuries BCE, the palace economies of the region broke down. Mycenaean Greece gave way to small village cultures, the Hittite empire collapsed, and Assyria and Egypt survived in weakened form.
How solid Scholars now see the collapse as more limited than older accounts claimed, because many supposed city destructions were misdated or never happened. There is no death toll.

kv.v: Many societies across Egypt, Anatolia, the Aegean, the Levant and Mesopotamia. Effects varied, and Cyprus saw little destruction.

Several, and still debated: drought and a cooler climate, invasions by the Sea Peoples, military change, the spread of iron, and possibly plague. Deep trade and diplomatic links meant that a disturbance in one place cascaded to others.
Greece entered the Dark Ages. Phoenician city-states gained autonomy as Egyptian and Assyrian power waned.

items.solid: How solid Scholars now see the collapse as more limited than older accounts claimed, because many supposed city destructions were misdated or never happened. There is no death toll.

p: Mediterranean, Near East, Europe
Plague reached Roman Egypt in 541 and by 543 had spread to every corner of Justinian's empire. Constantinople lost about a fifth of its people by one account and up to 40 percent by another.

How solid Heavily debated. Revisionist historians argue that the plague caused high mortality in some places but no widespread demographic decline. Procopius reported 10,000 deaths a day in Constantinople, a figure whose accuracy is in question.

kv.v: Contemporary sources say it came on rats and fleas aboard grain ships from Egypt, a major import for the Byzantines.
For the first plague pandemic as a whole, some historians estimate 15 to 100 million deaths over two centuries.
The disease persisted in Northern Europe and Arabia until 549.

items.solid: How solid Heavily debated. Revisionist historians argue that the plague caused high mortality in some places but no widespread demographic decline. Procopius reported 10,000 deaths a day in Constantinople, a figure whose accuracy is in question.

p: Eurasia
Campaigns led by Genghis Khan, Kublai Khan and Timur destroyed cities that resisted. Large areas of Central Asia and northeastern Persia were seriously depopulated.
How solid Weak. The estimates come from a book criticized for its methods and rely on Chinese censuses that are considered unreliable. Contemporary records are scarce.

kv.v: Possibly 20 to 60 million killed over two centuries, not counting Black Death deaths.
Military conquest.

items.solid: How solid Weak. The estimates come from a book criticized for its methods and rely on Chinese censuses that are considered unreliable. Contemporary records are scarce.

p: Eurasia and North Africa
Plague reached Europe through the Genoese trading port of Caffa in Crimea and spread through the Mediterranean to North Africa, West Asia and the rest of Europe.
How solid Ranges are wide because few records survive. The highest and lowest totals differ by a factor of up to eight.

kv.v: Fleas on black rats aboard ships, moving through trading ports.

25 to 50 million deaths in one estimate, and 75 to 200 million across Eurasia in another. Europe lost 30 to 60 percent of its people by one account and 25 to 60 percent by another. About a third of the Middle Eastern population died.
Europe's population did not regain its 14th-century level until the 16th century.

items.solid: How solid Ranges are wide because few records survive. The highest and lowest totals differ by a factor of up to eight.

p: North and South America

After 1492, the Indigenous population of the Americas fell sharply. Lower estimates imply a decline of about 80 percent by the late 17th century in Central and South America, and some researchers say about 90 percent within a century of Columbus's arrival.
How solid Weak. The estimates are extrapolations from small bits of data. A 2020 genetic study suggests earlier Caribbean estimates may have been at least tenfold too large.

kv.v: Pre-contact estimates run from 8 to 112 million, with recent ones mostly between 45 and 60 million. Regional figures include a 50 to 80 percent die-off in 16th-century Mexico and a drop in Brazil from about 4 million to 300,000.
Epidemic disease, enslavement, war, forced labor and displacement. Scholars disagree about the weight of each, and many argue that colonial disruption made communities more vulnerable to disease.

items.solid: How solid Weak. The estimates are extrapolations from small bits of data. A 2020 genetic study suggests earlier Caribbean estimates may have been at least tenfold too large.

p: Africa to the Americas
About 12.75 million Africans were loaded onto slave ships bound for the Americas, by the current estimate. The trade peaked in the last two decades of the 18th century.
How solid The embarkation figure rests on ship records, though studies differ (about 12 million in one, 12.75 million in another). Deaths inside Africa are a much weaker estimate.

kv.v: Up to 2 million died on the voyage. Another historian estimates that about 4 million more died inside Africa after capture, which gives roughly 1.5 to 5.5 million deaths depending on what is counted (my arithmetic).
An organized human trade.
Britain banned the trade in 1807, and participating nations had completely banned it by 1853.

items.solid: How solid The embarkation figure rests on ship records, though studies differ (about 12 million in one, 12.75 million in another). Deaths inside Africa are a much weaker estimate.

items.h3: Tambora and the year without a summer
p: Indonesia and the Northern Hemisphere

The 1815 eruption of Tambora rated VEI 7 and is the most recent confirmed eruption of that size. It lowered the global average temperature by 0.4 to 0.7 °C, and in 1816 harvests failed across New England and Europe.
How solid The source gives no overall death toll.

kv.v: In New England, no more than a quarter of the corn ripened enough to use for food. Wheat, oat and potato harvests failed in Britain and Ireland.
Typhus epidemics followed the famine between 1816 and 1819, and more than 65,000 people died as the disease spread out of Ireland. The cooling itself was temporary.

items.solid: How solid The source gives no overall death toll.

p: Ireland
Potato blight, which probably arrived in 1844, struck a population that depended on a single crop and on absentee landlords. The worst year was 1847.
How solid One million is the most widely accepted death toll, with a plausible range of half a million to one and a half million.

kv.v: About 1 million deaths, within a plausible range of 0.5 to 1.5 million, and more than 1 million emigrants. At least 2.1 million people left Ireland between 1845 and 1855.
Blight, made far worse by landlordism and dependence on one crop. The government followed a laissez-faire policy and ended earlier relief, and large food exports continued.

Ireland's population fell 20 to 25 percent between 1841 and 1871, from about 8.5 million before the famine to 4.4 million by 1901. Marriage ages rose, and a third of Irish men and a quarter of Irish women never married.

items.solid: How solid One million is the most widely accepted death toll, with a plausible range of half a million to one and a half million.

p: China

A civil war between the Qing dynasty and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, whose capital Nanjing fell in 1864. About 30 million people fled the conquered regions, and the last rebel forces were defeated in 1871.
How solid Speculative. There was no reliable census, and only about 10 percent of Taiping records survive.

kv.v: The most widely cited estimate is 20 to 30 million deaths, which the source puts at 5 to 10 percent of China's population. Higher estimates run from 73 to 100 million.

items.solid: How solid Speculative. There was no reliable census, and only about 10 percent of Taiping records survive.

p: Worldwide
Smallpox was still killing people at scale in the 1900s. Ordinary smallpox killed about 30 percent of those infected.
How solid Estimates vary widely.

kv.v: 250 to 500 million deaths in the 20th century by one estimate. Another figure often quoted is up to 300 million.
A virus spreading from person to person.
The WHO certified global eradication in May 1980.

items.solid: How solid Estimates vary widely.

items.meta: Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia
p: Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia
A war among industrial powers killed 15 to 22 million people, military and civilian combined.
How solid The share is calculated against the countries listed in the source, not the world population.

kv.v: About 1.7 to 2.3 percent of the population of the countries involved, which together held 959.7 million people.

items.solid: How solid The share is calculated against the countries listed in the source, not the world population.

p: Worldwide

The pandemic is conventionally dated from a case at Camp Funston, Kansas, on 4 March 1918. The virus spread with troop movements to other American camps and to Europe, reaching the Western Front by mid-April.
How solid Weak at the edges. Limited data leave the origin uncertain, estimates for China are unreliable, and the authors of one Russian estimate (450,000 deaths) called it a shot in the dark.

kv.v: A second wave likely reached Boston and Freetown, Sierra Leone, by ship from Brest. After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, released Russian prisoners of war carried the disease home.
About 500 million people were infected, nearly a third of the world's population. Deaths of 25 to 50 million are generally accepted, with other estimates from 17 million to 100 million.

items.solid: How solid Weak at the edges. Limited data leave the origin uncertain, estimates for China are unreliable, and the authors of one Russian estimate (450,000 deaths) called it a shot in the dark.

p: Worldwide
The deadliest conflict in the record, including deaths from deprivation, famine and disease.
How solid The two ranges in the source differ, so the share is 3.0 to 3.7 percent depending on which is used.

kv.v: 60 to 75 million deaths in one estimate and 70 to 85 million in another, about 3 percent of the 2.3 billion people alive in 1940.

items.solid: How solid The two ranges in the source differ, so the share is 3.0 to 3.7 percent depending on which is used.

p: Bengal, British India

Famine struck Bengal, a province of about 60 million people, during the Second World War. The fall of Burma cut off rice imports, a cyclone and crop disease reduced the 1942 harvest, and British wartime denial policies removed rice and seized about 45,000 boats.
How solid The death toll is accepted within a range. The causes are actively disputed.

kv.v: Estimated deaths range from 0.8 to 3.8 million, and the scholarly consensus is about 2.1 million.

Debated. The Famine Inquiry Commission called it a crisis of the distribution of food and income, not of availability. Amartya Sen argued that the 1943 rice supply was only about 5 percent below the previous five-year average, while others estimated shortfalls of 20 to 33 percent. Wartime inflation cut real wages, and historians disagree about the role of the British War Cabinet in refusing or cutting import requests.

items.solid: How solid The death toll is accepted within a range. The causes are actively disputed.

p: China

Famine deaths began in 1958 and lasted until 1962, with the core period from 1959 to 1961. Harvests fell 15 percent in 1959 against 1958, and 1960 output was about 70 percent of the 1958 level. Grain exports continued.
How solid Highly disputed. Scholars have criticized several of the highest estimates for weak methods.

kv.v: The commonly cited range is 15 to 46 million excess deaths. Newer estimates cluster around 30 to 46 million, and published estimates run from 3.5 million to 55 million.

Government policy, including the Great Leap Forward, communes, extreme grain procurement and overreported grain output, together with drought and floods. One study attributes 69 percent of deaths to policy and 31 percent to natural disasters, and the weather's role is debated.

items.solid: How solid Highly disputed. Scholars have criticized several of the highest estimates for weak methods.

p: Bhopal, India

On 2 and 3 December 1984, methyl isocyanate gas escaped from a storage tank at the Union Carbide pesticide plant after water entered the tank and set off a runaway reaction. More than 500,000 people were exposed.
How solid Estimates of the death toll differ by a factor of about seven.

kv.v: Official immediate deaths were 2,259, and the Madhya Pradesh government later confirmed 3,787. Other estimates run to about 8,000 within two weeks plus 8,000 or more from gas-related disease, and some claims exceed 16,000. A 2006 government affidavit reported at least 558,125 injuries, about 3,900 of them severe and permanently disabling.
An overfilled tank, malfunctioning safety systems and poor maintenance. How the water entered is disputed: investigators cite pipe cleaning, and the company cites sabotage.

items.solid: How solid Estimates of the death toll differ by a factor of about seven.

p: Ukraine, then the Soviet Union

On 26 April 1986, reactor 4 exploded during a safety test, started a core fire and spread radioactive contamination across the Soviet Union and Europe. It is rated level 7, the maximum on the international scale.

How solid Long-term deaths are contested. The UN figure is up to 4,000 in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia, other assessments reach 16,000 across Europe, and a few studies propose hundreds of thousands, which are widely disputed on method.

kv.v: Two workers died in the explosions and 28 more of acute radiation syndrome within three months. About 135,000 people were evacuated long term, about 100,000 square kilometres were contaminated, and the exclusion zone covers about 2,600 square kilometres.
Reactor design flaws and operator actions.

items.solid: How solid Long-term deaths are contested. The UN figure is up to 4,000 in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia, other assessments reach 16,000 across Europe, and a few studies propose hundreds of thousands, which are widely disputed on method.

p: Worldwide
The WHO declared a pandemic about three months after the first reports.
How solid I read only the WHO headline, not the full report. Excess deaths are counted as deaths associated with the pandemic, so the figure covers more than deaths caused directly by the virus.

kv.v: The WHO estimated 14.9 million excess deaths associated with COVID-19 in 2020 and 2021.

items.solid: How solid I read only the WHO headline, not the full report. Excess deaths are counted as deaths associated with the pandemic, so the figure covers more than deaths caused directly by the virus.

patterns.h3: Connection carried disease
p: Each of the three great pandemics here travelled on the transport of its day: grain ships from Egypt in 541, Genoese trading ships in 1346, and troop movements and ships in 1918.

patterns.h3: Shortage became famine through decisions
p: In Ireland, food exports continued and earlier relief ended. In Bengal, wartime denial policies and inflation are cited, and in China, grain procurement and continued exports. In each case scholars dispute how much of the toll came from policy and how much from blight, weather or war.

patterns.h3: Recovery took generations, or did not come
p: Europe regained its pre-plague population in the 16th century. Ireland's decline lasted a century. Greece entered a dark age after the Bronze Age collapse. The cooling after Tambora, by contrast, was temporary.

patterns.h3: The numbers are soft
p: Totals for the Black Death differ by up to a factor of eight, for the 1918 influenza about six, for the Taiping Rebellion five, and for the Great Chinese Famine about sixteen. The older or more political the event, the wider the range.

patterns.h3: Industrial technology added a new kind of event
p: Bhopal and Chernobyl are the only industrial accidents here, and even on the high estimates their tolls are in the thousands to tens of thousands, not millions. The two world wars were fought by industrial states and killed 15 to 22 million and 60 to 85 million people.

patterns.h3: Most events were regional
p: The entries that reached across the world are the 1918 influenza, smallpox, COVID-19 and the world wars. The rest struck a region, a continent or an empire.

limits: The list is my selection. Nineteen events cannot cover the record.
Records are thinner for events outside Europe, East Asia and the Middle East, so the list probably understates the rest of the world.
Not covered: mass extinctions and other deep-time events, the Antonine plague, the 17th-century crises, and the many earthquakes, floods and regional famines that did not reach this scale.
A record kept by survivors lists only the catastrophes that humanity survived.

p: WHO's global network for tracking influenza has run since 1952. It now comprises 166 institutions across 136 WHO member states.

How solid WHO's own page. It gives the size and mission of the network but no performance data, and it does not say outright that the network selects vaccine strains; I infer that from the recommendations it publishes.

kv.v: Works as a global mechanism of surveillance, preparedness and response for seasonal, pandemic and zoonotic influenza, and as a global alert for novel influenza viruses and other respiratory pathogens.
Publishes vaccine composition recommendations, for example for the 2026–2027 northern hemisphere season.

items.solid: How solid WHO's own page. It gives the size and mission of the network but no performance data, and it does not say outright that the network selects vaccine strains; I infer that from the recommendations it publishes.

p: WHO estimates that immunization saved at least 154 million lives over 50 years, about six lives every minute of every year. Of these, 101 million were infants, and measles vaccine accounts for 60 percent, nearly 94 million.
How solid A modelled estimate published by WHO, measured against a world without vaccination. It is not a count of observed deaths.

kv.v: 84 percent of infants are protected with three DTP doses, up from fewer than 5 percent when the programme launched.
Vaccination against 14 diseases has directly contributed to reducing infant deaths by 40 percent globally and by more than 50 percent in the African Region.
Each life saved gained on average 66 years of full health, 10.2 billion in total.

items.solid: How solid A modelled estimate published by WHO, measured against a world without vaccination. It is not a count of observed deaths.

p: WHO certified global eradication in May 1980. Ordinary smallpox had killed about 30 percent of those infected.
How solid From Wikipedia, as in the record of catastrophes. Death estimates vary widely; the eradication date is not in dispute.

kv.v: An estimated 250 to 500 million deaths in the 20th century by one estimate, and up to 300 million by another.

items.solid: How solid From Wikipedia, as in the record of catastrophes. Death estimates vary widely; the eradication date is not in dispute.

p: Wild poliovirus cases have fallen by more than 99 percent since 1988, from an estimated 350,000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to two. Transmission continues in Afghanistan and Pakistan.
How solid WHO's own fact sheet. My read did not show the year of the latest count of two cases, or how many of the three wild types are eradicated.

kv.v: Over 20 million people are able to walk who would otherwise have been paralysed, according to WHO's immunization page.

items.solid: How solid WHO's own fact sheet. My read did not show the year of the latest count of two cases, or how many of the three wild types are eradicated.

p: The 78th World Health Assembly adopted the agreement by consensus. The day before, the committee approved it by 124 votes in favour, none against and 11 abstentions.
How solid WHO's own announcement. The agreement is not in force. See the section on thinning defenses for the annex.

kv.v: Principles and tools for coordinating prevention, preparedness and response, including equitable access to vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics. Manufacturers in the access system are to provide rapid access targeting 20 percent of their real-time production of pandemic vaccines.
It opens for signature only after the Assembly adopts an annex on pathogen access and benefit sharing. It enters into force after 60 ratifications.

items.solid: How solid WHO's own announcement. The agreement is not in force. See the section on thinning defenses for the annex.

p: Our World in Data lists major famines since 1990 in the Central African Republic, the DR Congo, Ethiopia, North Korea, Nigeria, Somalia and Sudan, and says recent famines have typically been far less deadly than earlier ones.
How solid The page gives per-decade totals only in charts, so the text figures are single famines. The 36 million figure sits inside the 15 to 46 million range used in the record of catastrophes.

kv.v: Its chart shows an estimated 36 million deaths in the Great Leap Forward famine, 1958 to 1962, and about 25 million in famines during the Second World War across the USSR, Europe and Asia.
About 340,000 estimated deaths in northeast Nigeria from 2016 to 2019.
The page credits more food per person, better markets and transport, healthcare and lower poverty, together with emergency aid and early-warning monitoring.

items.solid: How solid The page gives per-decade totals only in charts, so the text figures are single famines. The 36 million figure sits inside the 15 to 46 million range used in the record of catastrophes.

p: Opened in 2008 as a partnership between Norway's Ministry of Agriculture and Food, NordGen and the Crop Trust. It holds more than 1.4 million seed samples as of 2026, from 134 institutions, with room for 4.5 million.
How solid The Crop Trust's own page. It gives no data on how often the vault has been used.

kv.v: Described as the ultimate insurance policy for the world's food supply: it backs up crop collections so genebanks can restore them if the originals are lost or become inaccessible.

items.solid: How solid The Crop Trust's own page. It gives no data on how often the vault has been used.

p: A warning system for the Indian Ocean was up and running about eighteen months after the December 2004 tsunami, as scheduled, according to UNESCO's Director-General in 2006.
How solid A 2006 news report. It gives no figures on countries covered or on performance, so I have no outcome evidence for this system.

kv.v: It is a component of a global system and can receive and distribute tsunami advisories at all hours.

items.solid: How solid A 2006 news report. It gives no figures on countries covered or on performance, so I have no outcome evidence for this system.

p: Odisha's chief minister said a record 1.2 million people were evacuated in 24 hours. The UN disaster-risk office credited the almost pinpoint accuracy of the warnings for a well-targeted evacuation.
How solid One event, reported by Al Jazeera. The evacuation count is the state government's, and the article gives no evacuation figure for 1999.

kv.v: The article gives figures from 16 to 33 for the cyclone in India.
The 1999 super-cyclone in the same state killed more than 10,000 people.

items.solid: How solid One event, reported by Al Jazeera. The evacuation count is the state government's, and the article gives no evacuation figure for 1999.

p: Death rates from disasters have fallen by more than 90 percent over the last century, although the world has about four times as many people. Our World in Data says: “This is not because hazards have become weaker. It’s because societies have become more resilient.”

How solid The page warns that records from a century ago are incomplete, that early death rates may be underestimates, and that trends should not be inferred from pre-2000 data. The size of the fall is therefore uncertain.

kv.v: Weather forecasts and early warning, better buildings, national and international cooperation, and food systems that make a lost harvest less damaging.
Excluding extreme temperature, the typical figure for the last 10 to 15 years is roughly 10,000 to 20,000 deaths a year. In the 20th century, more than a million deaths in a year were not uncommon.

items.solid: How solid The page warns that records from a century ago are incomplete, that early death rates may be underestimates, and that trends should not be inferred from pre-2000 data. The size of the fall is therefore uncertain.

items.h3: Montreal Protocol and the ozone layer
p: The phase-out covers nearly 99 percent of banned ozone-depleting substances. If current policies stay in place, the ozone layer is expected to return to 1980 levels by about 2066 over the Antarctic, 2045 over the Arctic and 2040 for the rest of the world.
How solid From a WMO page. I did not check which edition of the assessment it summarizes or whether a newer one is out.

kv.v: The Kigali Amendment, which phases down some hydrofluorocarbons, is estimated to avoid 0.3 to 0.5 °C of warming by 2100, excluding HFC-23.

items.solid: How solid From a WMO page. I did not check which edition of the assessment it summarizes or whether a newer one is out.

items.h3: Cheaper clean power and the investment shift
p: IRENA reports that in 2024 solar photovoltaics were on average 41 percent cheaper than the lowest-cost fossil fuel alternatives, and onshore wind 53 percent cheaper. The IEA's World Energy Investment 2026 puts clean energy at about $2.2 trillion of roughly $3.4 trillion in global energy investment, against about $1.2 trillion for fossil fuels.

How solid Weak. Both sets of figures reached me secondhand, the IRENA ones through a trade-press summary and the IEA ones through an article citing a Forbes contributor. The IEA's own page gave no figures, and it says the 2026 estimates are shaped by an energy crisis tied to the conflict in the Middle East.

kv.v: Solar PV averaged $0.043 per kilowatt-hour in 2024. Battery storage prices fell 93 percent since 2010, to $192 per kilowatt-hour.
Nearly two dollars go to clean energy for every dollar committed to fossil fuels in 2026.

items.solid: How solid Weak. Both sets of figures reached me secondhand, the IRENA ones through a trade-press summary and the IEA ones through an article citing a Forbes contributor. The IEA's own page gave no figures, and it says the 2026 estimates are shaped by an energy crisis tied to the conflict in the Middle East.

p: Opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970. A total of 191 states have joined, including the five nuclear-weapon states.
How solid From the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs. The page lists the aims but does not report how many states have left or tried to acquire weapons.

kv.v: To prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and weapons technology, to promote cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, and to further the goal of nuclear disarmament and general and complete disarmament.

items.solid: How solid From the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs. The page lists the aims but does not report how many states have left or tried to acquire weapons.

p: The Federation of American Scientists puts the global inventory at about 70,300 warheads in 1986 and roughly 12,187 at the beginning of 2026, a fall of about 82 to 83 percent.
How solid Estimates by a research organization, not official counts. The page's two current figures differ by about 1 percent.

kv.v: The same page also gives 12,321 for the start of 2026 without reconciling the two. SIPRI's yearbook figure, used in the chapter on vulnerability, is 12,187.

items.solid: How solid Estimates by a research organization, not official counts. The page's two current figures differ by about 1 percent.

p: NASA's DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos, a small asteroid about 160 metres wide that orbits the larger asteroid Didymos. NASA announced on 11 October that the orbit had been shortened by 32 minutes.
How solid One test on one small asteroid, read through Space.com's report of NASA's announcement. It shows the method works once, not that it would work on a larger or faster body.

kv.v: The orbital period was 11 hours 55 minutes before the impact. NASA gave an uncertainty of two minutes either side of the 32-minute change.
The mission aimed for a change of at least 73 seconds, and scientists had hoped for about 10 minutes.
NASA's Lori Glaze said that for the first time humanity had changed the orbit of a planetary body. NASA knew of no large asteroid threatening Earth in the foreseeable future.

items.solid: How solid One test on one small asteroid, read through Space.com's report of NASA's announcement. It shows the method works once, not that it would work on a larger or faster body.

p: The known near-Earth object population is over 32,000 objects. A 2023 study in the Planetary Science Journal finds the near-Earth asteroid population about 38 percent complete for objects larger than 140 metres.
How solid I read the abstract only. The study is three years old, so completeness has probably risen, and I found no figure for objects over 1 kilometre.
items.solid: How solid I read the abstract only. The study is three years old, so completeness has probably risen, and I found no figure for objects over 1 kilometre.

p: The UN disarmament office says the convention effectively prohibits the development, production, acquisition, transfer, stockpiling and use of biological and toxin weapons. It was the first multilateral disarmament treaty to ban an entire category of weapons of mass destruction.
How solid The page I read gave no opening or entry-into-force dates, no count of member states, and does not mention verification, so I say nothing on those points.

kv.v: It relies primarily on a network approach of coordination with international, regional and non-governmental organizations.

items.solid: How solid The page I read gave no opening or entry-into-force dates, no count of member states, and does not mention verification, so I say nothing on those points.

p: The second edition of a review of the science on general-purpose AI capabilities and risks. It is led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, written by over 100 independent experts, and backed by over 30 countries and international organisations. Its partners are the UK AI Security Institute and Mila.
How solid The report informs decisions; it does not set rules. Who commissioned it was not stated on the page I read.

kv.v: To give decision-makers in government and beyond a shared, authoritative global picture of AI's risks and impacts.

items.solid: How solid The report informs decisions; it does not set rules. Who commissioned it was not stated on the page I read.

p: In force since 1 August 2024. The ban on certain AI systems has applied since 2 February 2025, and the obligations on general-purpose AI models since 2 August 2025.

How solid From an implementation-timeline site, last updated 31 August 2026. It does not mention any proposal to postpone these dates, so I cannot confirm whether one is under way. The law covers the EU, not the world.

kv.v: General-purpose models already on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027.
High-risk systems under Annex III must comply from 2 December 2027, those under Annex I from 2 August 2028, and some public-authority systems already on the market by 2 August 2030.

items.solid: How solid From an implementation-timeline site, last updated 31 August 2026. It does not mention any proposal to postpone these dates, so I cannot confirm whether one is under way. The law covers the EU, not the world.

patterns.h3: Routine systems produce the measured gains
p: The largest falls in the chart come from things done every day for decades: vaccination, forecasting, evacuation planning, food markets. Each has a long record that can be counted.

patterns.h3: Treaties hold while the parties stay
p: The NPT has 191 parties and the ozone phase-out reached nearly 99 percent. The lapse of New START and the US exit from WHO show that a defense of this kind can also be withdrawn.

patterns.h3: For the newest technologies the entries describe rules, not results
p: The AI safety report, the EU law and the biological weapons convention are descriptions of what exists. I found no figures in the sources showing a fall in harm from any of them.

patterns.h3: Many results are modelled or attributed loosely
p: The 154 million lives saved is a model, the disaster figure is flagged as uncertain by its own source, and the link between resilience and falling deaths is argued rather than measured.

limits: The list is my selection. Nineteen entries cannot cover every defense, and I left out areas such as building codes, hospital systems, financial safeguards and space weather monitoring.
Cause is hard to show. A fall in deaths may come from the defense, from wealth, or from both, and several sources say so only in general terms.
Several figures are secondhand: the IRENA and IEA numbers, the Cyclone Fani account and the DART report. They need checking against the original reports before use.
I did not find outcomes after mid-2026 for the pandemic annex, and I did not check whether the ozone assessment has been updated.
Defenses that worked without notice leave little trace in the record, so the list favours defenses with measurable results.
